summary: The Pulley calculator turns the pulley centers distance, the diameter and more into diameter (Driver pulley). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Editing anything puts the results away until the next press of Calculate — change one value at a time and the updated answer tells you what that value was worth.

sections.title: How does the Pulley calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pulley calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports diameter (Driver pulley) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the pulley centers distance, the diameter (Driven pulley), the angular velocity (Driven pulley) and the belt velocity.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pulley calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Diameter=angular velocity × diameter ÷ angular velocity
Belt length=(1 ÷ 4) × (2 × pulley centers distance × (PI × diameter + PI × diameter + 4 × pulley centers distance) + (diameter − diameter ^ 2)) ÷ pulley centers distance
Diameter=60 × belt velocity ÷ (PI × angular velocity)
Transmitting power=belt tension × belt velocity
Transmitting power=(1 ÷ 30) × PI × angular velocity × drive torque
Driven torque=30 × transmitting power ÷ (PI × angular velocity)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Angular velocity = 10 RPM and Diameter = 30 m. Working through the relationship above gives Diameter = 30 m and Belt velocity = 0.5655 m/s.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Diameter = 30 m and Belt velocity = 0.5655 m/s should be roughly the size you expected from Angular velocity = 10 RPM and Diameter = 30 m.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Power, opening in watts
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Frequency, opening in revolutions per minute
  • Torque, opening in newton meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Frequency, opening in revolutions per minute
  • Torque, opening in newton meters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pulley calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the pulley centers distance, the diameter and the angular velocity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pulley calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns diameter (Driver pulley), derived from the pulley centers distance, the diameter and the angular velocity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pulley calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pulley centers distance, the diameter, the angular velocity and the belt velocity, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter transmitting power in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Transmitting power opens in watts and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Diameter = 30 m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pulley calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
